1:
The opening verse is heard everywhere as an echo of the priestly benediction. Charles Ellicott calls it an adaptation of Numbers 6:24 with one deliberate change: where the formal benediction says upon us, the psalm has rather with, or among us. C.H. Spurgeon calls it a fit refrain to the High Priest’s blessing, and Adam Clarke that it is nearly the same form of words. Spurgeon marks where it begins: with a cry for mercy, forgiveness being the first link in the chain, so that the best saints and worst sinners may unite in the petition. Then the church begs a blessing: when we bless God we do but little, our blessings being words, but when God blesses he enriches us indeed, his being gifts and deeds. And still that is not all, for his people pray besides for a smile from his face.

Matthew Henry fastens on the plural: the psalmist does not pray God be merciful to me, but to us, as our Saviour in teaching us to say Our Father intimated that we ought to pray with and for others. He takes the clauses as a sequence: our happiness rises in God’s mercy, which is why mercy is asked first, and asked by sinners, as at Luke 18:13; it is conveyed by his blessing, his speaking well to us amounting to his doing well for us; and completed in the light of his countenance.

What occasion produced it they cannot settle. John Calvin reports three guesses — Bishop Patrick’s, that David composed it after bringing the ark to Jerusalem; Horsley’s, that it is a tabernacles hymn; and Calmet’s, that it followed the return from Babylon, when fertility was restored after the drought recorded by Haggai — but holds that whatever the occasion it is a prayer of the ancient church for the appearance of the Messiah, agreeing with the old Jewish expositors. Adam Clarke takes the captivity view, that it was written at the return and foretells the Gentiles’ conversion. Keil and Delitzsch read it as a harvest psalm like the one before, but with the corn already gathered in rather than still standing, each harvest being to Israel a fulfilment of Leviticus 26:4 and a pledge that its mission to the world shall not go unaccomplished. They add a note on its build: seven stanzas, twice three of two lines with one of three between them forming the clasp of the septiad — appropriate, they observe, to a psalm the old expositors called the Old Testament Paternoster.

Augustine of Hippo recalls the two psalms before it, in which the soul was stirred up to bless the Lord: let our soul bless the Lord, and let God bless us, for both are profitable. First there is in us the blessing of the Lord, and the consequence is that we bless him — that the rain, this the fruit, rendered to God the Husbandman who rains upon us and tills us. We are at once his vineyard and his building, tilled for fruit and dwelt in by him who tills us.

The purpose clause of the second verse is read as mission. John Gill makes the way God’s method of grace in the salvation of sinners, made known by the apostles not only in Judea but throughout the whole earth. Adam Clarke glosses it as God’s way of justifying the ungodly and sanctifying the unholy. God’s way, he says, is God’s religion: what he walks in before men and men must walk in before him — and the whole gospel is called this way at Acts 19:9. John Wesley hears a strategy in it: deal so graciously with thy people that the Gentile world may at last be allured to join them. Charles Ellicott notes that the word rendered salvation is often better given as help, and that by health the translators meant healing power.
3:
The refrain divides them over whose mouths are meant. John Gill takes its first appearance of the Jews, who are to have occasion to praise God for the mission of Christ, and the verse that follows of the nations, who were glad and sang for joy when the gospel was preached to them. Adam Clarke refers the refrain itself to the Gentiles: when God’s way is made known upon earth they will praise him and give thanks for his unspeakable gift. Charles Ellicott adds only that the verb is better rendered give thanks.

What rule the nations are to be glad of turns on one word. Charles Ellicott reads the verbs as present rather than future, for thou judgest, and renders the second dost lead, the word used at Psalm 23:3 of the pastoral care of God. John Wesley reaches the same sense and draws the contrast out: the Hebrew is lead, and it means gently, as a shepherd does his sheep, not with rigour as other lords had done. Adam Clarke takes it institutionally. Even the political state of the nations shall be greatly meliorated, for God will be acknowledged the supreme Judge, their laws founded on his word, and they governed according to judgment, justice and equity. On the Selah he writes simply that this is true and that innumerable facts confirm it: all the nations which have received the gospel have been benefited politically as well as spiritually.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the ground of the prospect from the present. The expectation of the conversion of the heathen receives as its foundation a joyous event of the moment: the earth has just yielded its fruit, the fruit that had been sown and hoped for. That increase is at once a blessing and an earnest of further blessing, by virtue of which all peoples to the uttermost bounds of the earth shall reverence the God of Israel. And they state the principle behind it: it is the way of God that all the good he manifests towards Israel shall be for the well-being of mankind.

The repetition of the refrain is accounted for two ways. John Gill takes it as showing the ardour of the church’s mind and the fervency of her petitions, or else as declaring the certainty of what she asks — which is how the Targum reads it, the people shall confess. Adam Clarke puts it more simply: seeing the abundance of blessings the Gentiles were to receive, the psalmist calls again and again upon them to magnify God.
6:
Whether the increase is literal is the question. John Gill takes it spiritually and rejects the alternative by name: not literally the land of Israel, as some copies of the Targum have it and as Kimchi interprets, but mystically the church of God in the times of the Messiah. The word of God preached in the world is the seed sown in it, converts to Christ are the increase, and the church is God’s husbandry where that increase is brought forth. It had its accomplishment in part in the first times of the gospel, has been fulfilling more or less ever since, and will appear more abundantly in the latter day, when a plentiful harvest of souls shall be brought in, both Jews and Gentiles. He allows a second sense too, of the fruitfulness of believers, who may themselves be called earth.

Adam Clarke keeps the soil literal and supplies a mechanism. The ground was cursed for the sin of man, and the curse was to be removed by Jesus Christ; the fertility of the ground should therefore be influenced by the preaching of the gospel, since as minds become enlightened by the truth they become capable of the most beneficial discoveries in arts and sciences, and there should be an especial blessing on the toil of the pious husbandman. Wherever true religion prevails, he concludes, everything partakes of its beneficent influence. John Wesley takes the same order of cause and effect more simply: when the people of the earth are converted, God will cause it to yield them abundance of all sorts of fruits, under which one blessing all others, temporal and spiritual, are comprehended; and the God named as our own is Israel’s God in a peculiar manner.

Charles Ellicott alone disputes the tense. It seems to him more in keeping with an expression of thanks to render the clause with the Greek and Latin as a statement about the past — the land hath yielded her increase — rather than as a promise of what shall be.

The closing benediction draws two observations from Adam Clarke. The first is a matter of division: the last clause of the sixth verse should be joined to the seventh, as it is in several versions and should be in all. The second is doctrinal. Many of the fathers and several commentators have thought there is a reference to the Holy Trinity in the triple repetition of the divine name — God, our God, shall bless us; God shall bless us — and he gives the Old Psalter’s paraphrase, which distributes the three blessings to the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost, so that all the ends of the earth may dread him who will come to judge rightly what was judged unrightly. John Gill assigns the blessing of the last verse to the Spirit in particular, who blesses with regenerating grace, with faith, comfort and peace, by shedding abroad in the heart the love of the Father and the Son, applying precious promises and testifying adoption.

Of the psalm as a whole he says that when or by whom it was written cannot be ascertained, that it seems simply a prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles, and that it is so fine a piece of devotion that it would be nearly impossible to repeat it with a cold heart.
